results.message: Why did your bishops meet in councils?

voice_event.speaker: lpc
voice_event.text:
Our bishops met to decide disputes that touched us all -- disputes we could not leave undecided, and would not settle by breaking communion. A bishop meets other bishops because he answers for his own people, and what his people face, others face too. The question presses on every congregation, and the table holds them together when they disagree about the answer.

Our sharpest dispute was over the font, and we brought it to council twice. Cyprian's council in 256 ruled that baptism given outside the church is nothing at all. At that same council, Cyprian opened with a plain rule: “None of us sets himself up as a bishop over other bishops, and none of us uses a tyrant's terror to force a colleague into obedience. Every bishop has his own right to judge, in keeping with the freedom and power allowed to him. He can no more be judged by another bishop than he himself can judge another. Instead, let us all wait for the judgment of our Lord Jesus Christ. He is the only one who has the power both to place us in the government of His Church and to judge how we conduct ourselves there.”

A century and a half later, Augustine argued at book length that Cyprian's ruling was wrong. He never once put Cyprian outside our communion.

The councils were already standing when both bishops took their seats. They did not have to be built. They could meet because the church was organized enough to hold real factions and still call dozens of bishops together. That is why disagreement did not have to end in a split.

glosses.plain_meaning: For us, communion is a formal standing within the one body. You can lose it, and be given it back. At the council of 256, Cyprian said no one would be put out of it for thinking differently.
glosses.quick_meaning: For us, communion is a real standing inside the one body. You can lose it, and be given it back. Cyprian held that it should survive sharp disagreement.
glosses.translational_sense: A modern listener is likely to hear either a specific liturgical rite -- going up to receive -- or a general warmth of fellowship, and the second makes disagreement look like a failure of communion. We mean a formal, structural status of standing within the body, with public consequences, that, on Cyprian's own principle, disagreement should not dissolve. Disagreement is expected among us; what would break communion is not arguing but separating.
false_friend: a specific liturgical rite alone, going up to receive, with no broader sense of standing attached
a general warmth of fellowship and mutual good feeling, so that any real disagreement looks like a failure of it

names.name: Thascius Caecilius Cyprianus, bishop of Carthage (248/249-258)

figures_used.bridge_line: Our bishop, chosen while still new to the faith, over his own reluctance. During a plague he taught us to love even our enemies. He was put to death under Valerian.

dates.display: a trained rhetorician who turned from a public career to Christian life, converted c. 246; ordained and elected bishop of Carthage between roughly July 248 and April 249 by the acclamation of the Carthaginian people, over the recorded opposition of five presbyters, while still newly baptised (Doc_01 SS2; lpc.story.election-of-cyprian); banished to Curubis under the Valerianic persecution; executed under the emperor Valerian in 258 (lpc.story.the-death-of-cyprian)

names.name: Augustinius of Hippo Regius, presbyter 391, bishop 395/396-430

figures_used.bridge_line: Our bishop at Hippo. The people seized him and brought him to be made a presbyter while he wept. Later they pressed him into the bishop's office over his own refusal. He spent his last days weeping over psalms of penitence, while an army lay outside the walls.

dates.display: converted 386, baptised 387; seized by the congregation at Hippo and ordained presbyter against his own wishes in 391, weeping through it (Possidius, Vita IV, independently re-located this session; Doc_01 SS2); designated coadjutor and consecrated bishop of Hippo by Megalius, primate of Numidia, in 395/396, again amid popular acclamation (Possidius, Vita VIII; Doc_01 SS2); died 430, during the Vandal siege of Hippo (lpc.story.the-psalms-on-the-wall)

elements.surface: “None of us sets himself up as a bishop over other bishops, and none of us uses a tyrant's terror to force a colleague into obedience. Every bishop has his own right to judge, in keeping with the freedom and power allowed to him. He can no more be judged by another bishop than he himself can judge another. Instead, let us all wait for the judgment of our Lord Jesus Christ. He is the only one who has the power both to place us in the government of His Church and to judge how we conduct ourselves there.”
